title: Constipation (Vibandha): Ayurvedic Causes, Diet & Daily Routine
excerpt: Bowels not clearing, hard stools, straining and heaviness in the stomach — constipation is a very common problem. Learn its causes from the Ayurvedic view, what to eat and what to avoid, the right daily routine, yoga, safe home remedies, how to avoid the laxative habit, and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“My stomach does not clear in the morning, and I feel heavy the whole day” — this complaint is heard in almost every home. Constipation looks like a small problem, but if it lasts a long time it can lead to gas, loss of appetite, headache, irritability, piles and fissures.

The good news is that in most people constipation improves a great deal with diet, water, daily routine and correct toilet habits. This article is for information only — take treatment only on the advice of your Vaidya or doctor.

What is constipation?

Every person's bowel pattern is different — some go once a day, some twice, and some every other day. So simply “not going every day” is not constipation. Generally, these situations are considered constipation:

  • Passing stools fewer than 3 times a week
  • Stools that are dry, hard or lumpy
  • Straining hard or having pain while passing stools
  • A feeling that the bowel has not fully emptied even after the toilet

Constipation for a few days is often due to a change in food or routine and settles on its own. But if it continues for many weeks or months, it is called chronic constipation, and knowing the right cause becomes important.

The Ayurvedic view

In Ayurveda, constipation is called Vibandha or Malavarodha. Its main cause is a disturbance of Apana Vayu in the large intestine (Pakvashaya) — the same Vayu that moves stool, urine and gas downwards. When dry, cold, stale or very little food is eaten, too little water is drunk, one stays awake late at night or holds back the urge to pass stools, Vata increases and dries the intestines, and the stool dries up and gets stuck. Ama (undigested residue) formed due to weak Agni also sticks in the intestines and increases Vibandha.

Acharya Charaka has clearly forbidden suppressing the natural urges:

न वेगान्धारयेद्धीमाञ्जातान्मूत्रपुरीषयोः ।
न रेतसो न वातस्य न छर्द्याः क्षवथोर्न च ॥
— Charaka Samhita, Sutra Sthana 7

Meaning: A wise person should not suppress the urges of urine, stool, semen, flatus (gas), vomiting and sneezing once they arise. In today's rush, repeatedly postponing the urge to pass stools is itself a big cause of constipation.

So in Ayurveda, the basis of caring for constipation is — calming Vata, keeping Agni balanced, maintaining snigdhata (lubrication) in the intestines and respecting the natural urges.

Main causes

  • Lack of fibre in food — too much maida, biscuits and fast food; too little fruit, vegetables, pulses and whole grains
  • Drinking too little water and fluids, especially in winter
  • Lack of physical activity, sitting for long hours
  • Holding back the urge, rushing in the toilet, travel and changes in routine
  • Staying up late at night, irregular meal times and mental stress
  • Some medicines — such as iron and calcium tablets, some painkillers, antacids, and some medicines for depression and BP
  • Some diseases — low thyroid, diabetes, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), piles-fissure (avoiding the toilet for fear of pain), Parkinson's disease
  • Pregnancy and older age; the habit of taking laxatives again and again

Symptoms

  • Stools that are hard, dry or in lumps
  • Straining and taking a long time in the toilet
  • Heaviness, bloating, gas and mild pain in the abdomen
  • Reduced appetite, bad taste in the mouth, white coating on the tongue
  • Headache, sluggishness, irritability and poor sleep
  • Pain, burning or a little blood at the anus from straining (a sign of fissure or piles)

Tests

Ordinary constipation usually does not need any major test — the doctor or Vaidya understands the cause by asking about your food, routine and medicines and by examining the abdomen. But in chronic constipation or when there are warning signs, blood tests (haemoglobin, thyroid — TSH, sugar, calcium), a test for hidden blood in the stool, and if needed a colonoscopy may be done — especially when constipation starts suddenly after the age of 45–50.

Diet: what to eat, what to avoid

The aim of the diet is — to give the intestines fibre and moisture, calm Vata and keep Agni balanced. Take food that is fresh, warm and on time.

What to eat

  • Enough water through the day — drinking lukewarm water on waking is helpful for many people (in kidney or heart disease ask your doctor about the amount of water)
  • Green leafy and fibre-rich vegetables — bottle gourd, ridge gourd, spinach, fenugreek leaves, carrot, beetroot, pointed gourd
  • Fruits — papaya, guava, pear, apple, fig, orange; soaked raisins or munakka
  • Whole grains — atta with bran, dalia (broken wheat), jowar, bajra; pulses with husk and moong khichdi
  • A little desi ghee or sesame oil in food — according to Ayurveda it keeps the intestines lubricated (in heart disease or high cholesterol ask your doctor)
  • Fresh thin buttermilk with roasted cumin along with lunch

What to avoid

  • Maida, biscuits, bread, pizza, noodles and packaged snacks
  • Very oily-fried, stale, cold and dry food
  • Too much tea-coffee and alcohol — they reduce water in the body
  • Skipping meals or eating very little; eating again and again without hunger

Do not increase fibre suddenly — increase it slowly and increase water along with it, otherwise gas and bloating may increase.

Daily routine and yoga

In Ayurveda, Dinacharya (daily routine) is considered the foundation of health. In constipation the most benefit comes from regularity:

  • Sleep and wake at the same time every day; wake up early in the morning
  • Make unhurried time for the toilet after waking and after breakfast; never postpone the urge when it comes
  • Keep a small stool under your feet in the toilet so that the knees stay above the hips — this makes passing stools easier
  • At least 30 minutes of brisk walking or some exercise daily; walk 100 steps after meals
  • Keep meal times regular; dinner light and 2–3 hours before sleeping

Yoga and pranayama

Pavanamuktasana, Malasana, Vajrasana (after meals), Bhujangasana and Anulom-Vilom are considered helpful in constipation. Caution: in pregnancy, hernia, recent abdominal surgery, knee pain or heart disease, ask your doctor first; the elderly should do them slowly and with support. Learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe home remedies

  • Lukewarm water: one or two glasses of lukewarm water on an empty stomach in the morning
  • Soaked raisins or figs: soak at night and eat in the morning (keep the amount small in diabetes)
  • Papaya: ripe papaya in the morning or afternoon
  • Isabgol husk: with enough water or milk — never take it without water, and keep a gap of about 2 hours from other medicines
  • Abdominal massage: gentle clockwise massage around the navel with lukewarm sesame oil

These remedies are only supportive. If there is no improvement in two to three weeks, see a Vaidya or doctor.

Ayurvedic herbs — with caution

Ayurveda mentions several medicines for Vibandha, such as Triphala, Haritaki (harad), Amaltas (Aragvadha), Senna (sanay), Eranda taila (castor oil) and classical formulations like Panchasakar churna. For chronic constipation, Basti (a Panchakarma procedure) under a Vaidya's supervision is also mentioned. However:

  • Which medicine, in what dose and for how long — the Vaidya decides this only after looking at each person's prakriti, pulse, age, the cause of constipation and current medicines.
  • Do not stop your current medicines on your own — even if you feel the constipation is due to them. Discuss changing a medicine only with your doctor.
  • Do not take senna, castor oil and strong laxatives day after day for long periods — they can make the intestines lazy and cause loss of water and salts (potassium) from the body.
  • In pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and the elderly, give any laxative or medicine only on the advice of a Vaidya/doctor; in pregnancy never take strong laxatives or castor oil on your own. Beware of claims like “constipation removed from the root”.

When to see a doctor immediately

  • Blood in the stool or black stools
  • Unexplained weight loss, anaemia (low blood) or constant tiredness
  • Severe abdominal pain, swollen abdomen, vomiting and not even passing gas — go to hospital immediately
  • A sudden change in bowel habit after the age of 45–50, or a family history of bowel cancer
  • Fever with constipation, or constipation for more than three weeks despite medicines and remedies
  • In a newborn or small child, constipation since birth, a swollen abdomen, vomiting or not growing well

Summary — points to remember

  • Enough water, fibre-rich food, fruits and vegetables and whole grains
  • Never hold back the urge; go at the same time daily, without hurrying
  • Daily walking, exercise and yoga; do not stay awake late at night
  • Do not form a laxative habit; medicines only on the advice of an experienced Vaidya
  • If there is bleeding, weight loss or severe pain, see a doctor immediately
